Alain Prost :: Career legacy :: chunk_0016
Prost is widely regarded as one of Formula One's greatest-ever drivers. He is tied with [Sebastian Vettel](/wiki/Sebastian_Vettel "Sebastian Vettel") and [Max Verstappen](/wiki/Max_Verstappen "Max Verstappen") for the fourth-most Drivers' Championships of all time with four, behind only [Lewis Hamilton](/wiki/Lewis_Hamilton "Lewis Hamilton"), Michael Schumacher, and [Juan Manuel Fangio](/wiki/Juan_Manuel_Fangio "Juan Manuel Fangio").[[41]](#cite_note-:20-46) In addition, he was just 12.5 points away from an eight-title career.[[24]](#cite_note-:17-29) At his retirement, Prost held the record for most career Grand Prix victories (51),[[85]](#cite_note-90)[[1]](#cite_note-:2-2) which stood for fourteen years.[[86]](#cite_note-:0-91)[[87]](#cite_note-:13-92) ([Michael Schumacher](/wiki/Michael_Schumacher "Michael Schumacher") broke Prost's record during the [2001 season](/wiki/2001_Formula_One_World_Championship "2001 Formula One World Championship"). For his own part, Prost believed that had Ayrton Senna not [died in 1994](/wiki/1994_San_Marino_Grand_Prix "1994 San Marino Grand Prix"), he would have broken Prost's wins record first.[[86]](#cite_note-:0-91)) In addition, while Senna held the record for most career pole positions at Prost's retirement, Prost was superb on race day and held the record for most career [fastest laps](/wiki/Fastest_lap "Fastest lap") (41) until 2001, when Schumacher broke that record as well.[[88]](#cite_note-:27-93)

Prost currently shares the record for the highest percentage of races started from the front row in a single season (16 for 16 in [1993](/wiki/1993_Formula_One_World_Championship "1993 Formula One World Championship")) with [Ayrton Senna](/wiki/Ayrton_Senna "Ayrton Senna") ([1989](/wiki/1989_Formula_One_World_Championship "1989 Formula One World Championship")) and [Damon Hill](/wiki/Damon_Hill "Damon Hill") ([1996](/wiki/1996_Formula_One_World_Championship "1996 Formula One World Championship")).[[89]](#cite_note-94) As of 2026, he is the last Frenchman to have [won his home Grand Prix](/wiki/1993_French_Grand_Prix "1993 French Grand Prix").[[90]](#cite_note-95)

There are conflicting definitions of which states comprise the West Coast of the United States, but the West Coast always includes [California](/wiki/California "California"), [Oregon](/wiki/Oregon "Oregon"), and [Washington](/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)") as part of that definition. Under most circumstances, however, the term encompasses the three contiguous states and [Alaska](/wiki/Alaska "Alaska"), as they are all located in North America. For census purposes, [Hawaii](/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii") is part of the West Coast, along with the other four states.[[3]](#cite_note-World_Atlas_definition-4) *[Encyclopædia Britannica](/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica "Encyclopædia Britannica")* refers to the North American region as part of the Pacific Coast, including Alaska and [British Columbia](/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"). Although the encyclopedia acknowledges the inclusion of Hawaii in some capacity as part of the region, the editors wrote that "it has little in common geologically with the mainland states."[[4]](#cite_note-Encyclopædia_Britannica_article-5)

Several dictionaries offer different definitions of the West Coast. [Lexico](/wiki/Lexico "Lexico") restricts the West Coast's definition to "the western seaboard of the U.S. from Washington to California."[[5]](#cite_note-Lexico_definition-6) However, [Macmillan Dictionary](/wiki/Macmillan_Dictionary "Macmillan Dictionary") provides a less specific definition as "the western coast of the U.S., along the [Pacific Ocean](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean")."[[6]](#cite_note-Macmillan_definition-7) As for the [Cambridge Dictionary](/wiki/Cambridge_Advanced_Learner%27s_Dictionary "Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary"), the West Coast is "the area of the Pacific coast in the U.S. that includes California."[[7]](#cite_note-Cambridge_definition-8)

The Arabian Desert ecoregion has about 900 species of plants.[[8]](#cite_note-atlas-8) The Rub'al-Khali has very limited floristic [diversity](/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity"). There are only 37 plant species, 20 recorded in the main body of the sands and 17 around the outer margins. Of these 37 species, one or two are endemic. Vegetation is very diffuse but fairly evenly distributed, with some interruptions of near sterile dunes.[[2]](#cite_note-wwf-2) Some typical plants are *[Calligonum crinitum](/w/index.php?title=Calligonum_crinitum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Calligonum crinitum (page does not exist)")* on dune slopes, *[Cornulaca arabica](/w/index.php?title=Cornulaca_arabica&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cornulaca arabica (page does not exist)")* (saltbush), *[Salsola stocksii](/wiki/Salsola_stocksii "Salsola stocksii")* (saltbush), and *[Cyperus conglomeratus](/wiki/Cyperus_conglomeratus "Cyperus conglomeratus")*. Other widespread species are *[Dipterygium glaucum](/w/index.php?title=Dipterygium_glaucum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Dipterygium glaucum (page does not exist)"), [Limeum arabicum](/w/index.php?title=Limeum_arabicum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Limeum arabicum (page does not exist)")*, and *[Zygophyllum mandavillei](/w/index.php?title=Zygophyllum_mandavillei&action=edit&redlink=1 "Zygophyllum mandavillei (page does not exist)")*.

The highest peak, [Puncak Jaya](/wiki/Puncak_Jaya "Puncak Jaya") (4,884 metres (16,024 ft)), is located in the Sudirman Mountains. A string of volcanoes stretches from Sumatra to Nusa Tenggara,[[24]](#cite_note-24) then loops around through to the [Banda Islands](/wiki/Banda_Islands "Banda Islands") of Maluku to northeastern Sulawesi. Of the 400 volcanoes, approximately 150 are active.[[25]](#cite_note-gvp-25) Two of the most violent volcanic eruptions in modern times occurred in Indonesia; in 1815, [Mount Tambora](/wiki/Mount_Tambora "Mount Tambora") in [Sumbawa](/wiki/Sumbawa "Sumbawa") erupted, killing 92,000, and in 1883, [Krakatau](/wiki/Krakatau "Krakatau") erupted, killing 36,000. In 1970, Japanese mountaineers conducted a major expedition. The centrepiece was a large "siege"-style expedition, working on finding a new route up the Southwest Face.[[119]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUnsworth2000594-127) Another element was an attempt to ski Everest.[[97]](#cite_note-japtimes-105) Despite a staff of over one hundred and a decade of planning, the expedition suffered eight deaths and failed to summit.[[97]](#cite_note-japtimes-105) However, Japanese expeditions enjoyed some successes. [Yuichiro Miura](/wiki/Yuichiro_Miura "Yuichiro Miura") became the first man to ski down Everest from the South Col—he descended nearly 1,300 vertical metres (4,200 ft) from the South Col before falling with extreme injuries. Another success was an expedition that put four on the summit via the South Col route.[[97]](#cite_note-japtimes-105)[[120]](#cite_note-128)[[121]](#cite_note-129) Miura's exploits became the subject of film, and he went on to become the oldest person to summit Everest in 2003 aged 70 and in 2013 aged 80.[[122]](#cite_note-130)

In 1975, [Junko Tabei](/wiki/Junko_Tabei "Junko Tabei") became the first woman to summit Everest.[[97]](#cite_note-japtimes-105) The [1975 British Mount Everest Southwest Face expedition](/wiki/1975_British_Mount_Everest_Southwest_Face_expedition "1975 British Mount Everest Southwest Face expedition") led and organised by [Chris Bonington](/wiki/Chris_Bonington "Chris Bonington") made the first ascent of the Southwest Face from the [Western Cwm](/wiki/Western_Cwm "Western Cwm"). In 1978, [Reinhold Messner](/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner") and [Peter Habeler](/wiki/Peter_Habeler "Peter Habeler") made the first ascent of Everest without supplemental oxygen.
